Read the technical write-up

The analysis that shapes debate on reforms like the Milburn Review is static. It records who loses on the day the changes take effect and stops there. This tool starts from that static estimate and follows what happens next, as young people move into work, their pay rises and the economy grows.

1Immediate effect

The change in household incomes on day one, with behaviour held fixed, taken from PolicyEngine’s static estimate. Every line starts here.

2Moves into work

Young people moving into work, with pay and poverty paths observed in Understanding Society, net of tax and benefit withdrawal.

3Growth

The extra output of new workers, following OBR conventions, with the gain to the public finances shared out. It counts towards incomes and absolute poverty.

Starting point

On day one, the package takes around £1,000 a year from the average young person, and most from 18 and 19-year-olds

PolicyEngine’s static estimate shows how much household income each age loses when PIP and the health element of Universal Credit are withdrawn, before anyone changes what they do. Losses peak at 18 and 19 and are smallest at 16 and 17, because the package removes PIP from age 18. Averaged across all 7.5 million 16 to 24-year-olds, the loss is around £1,005 a year, or £7.5bn in total.

Source: PolicyEngine, Milburn report package, 2029-30. Average change in household income per young person, gainers and losers combined, before replacement payments.

That average hides who actually loses, which matters because only some of them can respond by moving into work.

1. Who loses

Two-thirds of the loss falls on young people already in work or education, who cannot respond by moving into work

Splitting young people into four groups shows where the loss lands. NEET young people not claiming lose nothing, the severely disabled are protected, and NEET young people who claim and lose can respond by moving into work. Young people in work or education lose most in total, but they are already working or studying. With the Youth Allowance and work allowance added back and losses phased in as claimants are reassessed, the first-year loss is the starting point for everything that follows.

From the immediate effect to living standards over time

The losses by group add up to the starting point, then moves into work and growth are layered on top.

By group, first year
Over time
Source: GGF calculations using PolicyEngine, Understanding Society, the Milburn Review and OBR conventions.

How quickly that loss is recovered depends on what young people earn once they start work.

2. What work is worth

Young people who start work see their pay rise fastest, so the gain from each job grows over time

Following young people in Understanding Society after they move into work shows that pay rises much faster for those who start young, around 50% in real terms over ten years for a 20-year-old against around 10% for someone starting at 42. Each new worker in the model follows this path, net of tax and the Universal Credit taper, so the employment effect keeps growing long after the jobs arrive.

Pay rises fastest for those who start young

Real hourly pay after entering work, entry = 100, by age at entry

Source: GGF calculations using Understanding Society.

Rising pay also lifts households out of poverty, which is where the static and long-run pictures differ most.

3. Poverty

A rise in poverty becomes a fall within a decade as young people move into work

Of young people in poverty who start work, two-thirds leave it in their first year, rising to 86% after six years in work. Each household that leaves poverty takes everyone in it out. Growth lowers absolute poverty further, but leaves relative poverty unchanged, because it lifts the poverty line along with incomes.

A rise in poverty becomes a fall as young people move into work

Change in people in poverty after housing costs, relative to no reform

Notes: Each exit counts everyone in the household. The DWP estimate is a cross-check, not used to set the model.

But the DWP’s 50,000 fall assumes every job is already filled, which raises the question of when it is actually reached.

4. Timing

How quickly young people move into work decides when poverty falls

The review phases its 440,000 extra jobs in over a decade, while the benefit changes are fully in place within around three years. If young people move into work on the review’s own timetable, poverty stays higher than without the reform for most of the first decade. If they move at the pace we observe in Understanding Society, the 50,000 fall comes around four years sooner.

The pace of moves into work decides when poverty falls

Change in relative poverty under two timetables for the same extra young people in work

Notes: DWP timetable follows the review’s NEET reduction profile, 2027/28 to 2036/37. GGF timetable follows observed moves into work in Understanding Society.

The end point is the same, but the path is not. The speed with which the Youth Guarantee and employment support reach young people matters as much to the package’s record on poverty as the benefit changes themselves, and that is something static analysis on its own cannot show.

Technical write-up

Beyond the morning after: how long-term effects change who wins and loses from the Milburn Review

The policy analysis that shapes public debate in the UK, produced by government and by independent think tanks and widely reported in the media, is static. It records who loses and who gains from a reform on the day it takes effect, with behaviour held fixed, and says nothing about what follows as people move into work and the economy grows. That analysis is transparent and quick to produce, which is why it frames how reforms are reported and judged, but it means reforms whose costs are immediate and concentrated, and whose benefits are delayed and widely shared, are judged on their costs alone.

This bias bears on two kinds of policy in particular, reforms with short-term losers but long-term winners, and reforms intended to raise growth, which almost always create some losers at the outset. Dynamic models that capture the later gains do exist, but they are laborious, usually applied by academics years after a policy has been enacted and confined to a handful of questions. Public debate is left with static analysis that is usable but incomplete, and dynamic analysis that is unusable when decisions are made.

The newly announced Milburn Review is exactly this kind of reform, since it withdraws Personal Independence Payment and the health element of Universal Credit from most under-25s, which on a static measure leaves young people worse off and pushes more of them into poverty, but its purpose is to move 440,000 more young people into work over the following decade1. This note sets out a model GGF has built to close the gap, taking the static estimate of a reform as given and adding an employment effect and a growth effect year by year, drawing on new analysis of Understanding Society (USOC) and the Office for Budget Responsibility’s own conventions, and applies it to the Milburn Review.

We find that adding the long-run gains from work and the growth this additional work generates fundamentally changes the interpretation of the package, turning a large immediate loss for young people and a sizeable rise in poverty into a fall in poverty within a decade and, eventually, a gain in young people’s incomes.

Key findings:

  • Static analysis misses most of the story for reforms that move people into work: including the review’s replacement payments, the Milburn Review package reduces young people’s household incomes by around £5.0bn a year on a static measure, but once moves into work and growth are counted the loss falls to around £0.4bn by year ten, and young people are better off each year from year 13.
  • A rise in poverty of 178,000 becomes a fall of around 120,000 by year ten: because two-thirds of young people in poverty who start work leave it in their first year, rising to 86% after six years in work, and the projection passes the DWP’s own estimate of 50,000 fewer people in poverty around year seven.
  • Two-thirds of the immediate loss falls on young people already in work or education: around £4.8bn a year, and they gain nothing from moves into work, which is why young people as a whole take more than a decade to come out ahead.
  • The growth effect is real, and how much reaches young people depends on the fiscal stance: the review’s 440,000 extra young people in work add around £22bn a year to GDP and around £10bn a year to the public finances by year ten, of which young people receive around £1.4bn a year when this Exchequer gain is returned to everyone equally, our central case.
  • Wages can fall as employment rises: an influx of young low-skilled workers on this scale could lower similar workers’ wages by around 3%, a cost that static analysis and simple dynamic scoring both miss.

1. Why static analysis holds back growth

Static distributional analysis calculates the change in each household’s income from a reform with employment, hours and wages held fixed, describing incomes on the morning after a reform rather than once people have responded. Official estimates of growth effects are produced separately by the OBR, usually only if the policy is part of a fiscal event and is above a threshold of 0.1% of potential output2, and they are rarely traced back to the households that bear the first-round losses.

As an example, the Mirrlees Review recommended abolishing stamp duty land tax and other inefficient taxes in 2011, warning that although some changes would be politically difficult, failure to reform imposes enduring costs3. Few have been enacted, which is naturally a consequence of political factors, but we argue is compounded by the methodological limitations of the way in which each reform would be assessed in public debate. Without a practical way of showing the gains alongside the losses, the case for reform is always argued at a disadvantage.

Key term: dynamic scoring

Dynamic scoring adds the behavioural and economic responses to a policy into the assessment of its effects. Static analysis assumes nobody changes what they do, whereas dynamic scoring allows for people moving into work, firms investing and the economy growing as a result. It is routine for major tax changes in the United States, but the models involved are slow and specialist, which is why they are rarely used when UK policy is being decided.

2. What the model does

2.1 Starting from the static estimate

Our model takes a package’s own static results as given, including the number of people affected, their cash change, broken down by group or by age, and the immediate change in poverty, so every projection matches the static figure at the start. We call this the immediate effect, and every later effect is measured against it, so the contribution of the employment and growth effects can be seen separately.

2.2 The employment effect, built on Understanding Society

Projecting what happens after someone moves into work needs data that follow the same people for many years. We link waves of Understanding Society from 2009-10 to 2023-24 and follow young people out of work to measure how often they move into work, what they earn, how their pay grows and whether their household leaves poverty4. Each new worker follows the measured pay path for their age, net of tax and the Universal Credit taper. The gradual build-up of moves into work matches the international evidence, with a review of more than 200 evaluations of employment programmes finding effects close to zero at first and growing over two to three years5. US evidence shows the response is concentrated among people with less severe conditions6, which is reflected in our finding that young people on disability benefits move into work at around a quarter of the rate of other young people out of work. Pay also rises much faster for those who enter work young, and the share of entrants who leave poverty keeps rising the longer they stay in work. Appendix A sets out how we built these estimates from Understanding Society, with the full results in Table A1 and Figures A1 and A2.

2.3 The growth effect, applying OBR principles to a subgroup

Turning extra employment into a growth effect that can be attributed to the people affected raises five questions, which the OBR answers for the economy as a whole but which have not previously been answered for a specific group of households. The model handles each in turn, and in every case it follows the spirit of OBR conventions where they exist and calibrates to the OBR’s aggregate results where they do not.

Does output rise with employment?

A key OBR assumption is that firms invest to equip new workers, so that capital per worker is unchanged and output rises in proportion to the number employed. If capital did not respond, each new worker would add less, and with labour receiving around 60% of national income the short-run growth effect would be around 40% smaller. The model adopts the OBR assumption and extends it beyond the OBR’s five-year forecast horizon, since the reforms it is designed to assess play out over a decade or more.

How productive are new workers?

The OBR assumes that people returning from health-related inactivity are around two-thirds as productive as the average worker7, a figure that reflects the earnings of a typical adult who left work through ill health. Young entrants earn around 40% of average pay, so applying the same ratio to them would credit each with output of around three times their pay, and would imply more extra GDP per job than the OBR’s own judgement that measures raising employment by 0.3% add around 0.2% to GDP because new joiners work fewer hours and earn less than average8.

The model handles this by starting each new worker at half of average output per worker, around £38,000 a year, and letting this rise in line with their measured pay as they gain experience. We chose this starting point because it reproduces in broad terms the relationship between employment and output that the OBR uses for the whole economy, around 0.67% more GDP for each 1% rise in employment. For the Milburn Review, the 440,000 extra workers raise employment by around 1.3% and GDP by around 0.8% by year ten, a little below the OBR ratio because many of the new workers have only recently started and their output rises with experience. Had we applied the OBR’s two-thirds assumption the same workers would have added around £29bn a year rather than £22bn, and assuming they were as productive as the average worker around £37bn. Across the economy the average worker produces around 1.7 times what they are paid, whereas our assumption already credits young entrants with around 2.5 times their pay, and studies linking firms’ output to their workers’ ages find that young workers’ pay is closely associated with what they produce9, so the higher assumptions would overstate the gain.

How much of extra output reaches households?

Not every pound of GDP becomes household income, since part goes to depreciation, overseas investors and retained profits. The model therefore converts extra output into household disposable income, around 60% of GDP and the measure closest to the real incomes used in distributional analysis, and then deducts the new workers’ own gross pay, because their earnings are already counted in the employment effect and would otherwise be counted twice.

Who receives the growth, and what happens to the Exchequer gain?

Extra employment also improves the public finances, since new workers pay tax and claim less in benefits and the wider output they generate is taxed, a gain of around £10bn a year by year ten for the Milburn Review package. What happens to this Exchequer gain is a decision for government rather than an economic effect, so the model offers three options. Our central case assumes the gain is returned to everyone equally, for example through lower taxes or higher spending, so young people, around 11% of the population, receive their share of around £1.4bn a year by year ten. If the Exchequer instead retains the gain to reduce borrowing, young people gain around £0.3bn, whereas if the gain from the new workers themselves is recycled to young people, they gain around £6.5bn a year and are better off from around year six. While the latter is generous, it is reasonable as a scenario as government may wish to compensate a group that has lost out with the induced tax revenues, as it did in the Autumn Budget 2021 when, weeks after ending the £20-a-week uplift to Universal Credit, it cut the taper rate from 63% to 55%10.

How does growth affect poverty?

Growth raises incomes across the population, including at the median, so it leaves relative poverty unchanged while reducing absolute poverty, which is measured against a line fixed in real terms. The model therefore applies the growth effect to absolute poverty only, and attributes all of the change in relative poverty to people moving into work.

3. Applying the model to the Milburn Review

Our starting point is the static estimate of what the package takes from young people on the day it takes effect. Before any replacement payments, PolicyEngine estimates that the average 16 to 24-year-old loses around £1,005 a year in household income, with losses peaking at 18 and 19 and smallest at 16 and 17, because the package removes PIP from age 18 (Figure 1).

Figure 1: On day one, losses peak at 18 and 19

Static change in household income per young person by age, Milburn Review package, £ a year, 2029-30

Notes: PolicyEngine static estimate with benefits withdrawn and no replacement payments. Gainers and losers combined.

Source: PolicyEngine.

Behind that average, we use PolicyEngine’s estimate for 2029-30, which models every household in the Family Resources Survey and splits all 7.5 million 16 to 24-year-olds by whether they are NEET or in work or education11. We use four groups, because each responds to the package differently. NEET young people not claiming the affected benefits lose nothing but can move into work. NEET young people who are severely disabled would move onto the review’s Severe and Complex Needs Insurance, paid above today’s maximum awards, so they gain rather than lose. NEET young people who claim and lose can move into work, while young people already in work or education lose cash but have no further move into work to make. We then add the review’s replacement payments. PolicyEngine models the higher Youth Allowance and work allowance directly, worth around £0.9bn a year, but the Severe and Complex Needs Insurance, the Additional Cost Allowance and the Health and Disability Fund have no published rates. We value these together at around £1.25bn a year, the gap between PolicyEngine’s estimate and the review’s own net saving, and as a best guess until they are costed we allocate around £0.5bn to severely disabled NEET young people and around £0.75bn to other young people who lose out. With these included, the immediate effect of the whole package is around −£5.0bn a year once fully in place, or around £660 per young person.

Figure 2: Most of the loss falls on young people already in work or education

Immediate effect of the whole Milburn Review package by group, first year, £ a year

We then phase the losses in as claimants are reassessed, following PolicyEngine’s own phased run, with 59% of the full loss in the first year, 84% in the second, 93% in the third and all of it from the fourth, which is why our first-year rise in poverty of around 90,000 is lower than the 178,000 the whole package produces at full effect. The review’s 440,000 extra young people in work are phased in as the review sets out, around 5% in the first year, 56% by year five and all by year ten, and each household that leaves poverty takes everyone in it out, counted at 2.4 people per household, PolicyEngine’s own ratio for losing households, so the employment effect is on the same basis as the starting estimate.

Figure 3: Moving into work and growth turn a large loss into a gain over time

Change in the household incomes of all 16 to 24-year-olds from the whole Milburn Review package, relative to no reform, £ a year, 2024 prices

Notes: Losses phased in over four years, 440,000 extra young people in work phased in as in the review, Exchequer gain returned to everyone.

Source: GGF Calculations using PolicyEngine, Understanding Society, the Milburn Review and OBR conventions.

Figure 3 shows that the immediate effect substantially overstates the long-run cost to young people. As moves into work build up, the employment effect cuts the £5.0bn loss to around £1.8bn by year ten, and growth reduces it to around £0.4bn, with young people as a whole better off each year from year 13. The recovery is slower than for a reform targeted only at people out of work, because two-thirds of the loss falls on young people already in work or education, who gain nothing from moves into work.

Incomes, with work and growth −£2.4bn −£4.0bn −£0.4bn +£1.9bn

Source: GGF Calculations using PolicyEngine, Understanding Society, the Milburn Review and OBR conventions.

The poverty results are where the dynamic picture differs most from the static one. Poverty rises by 178,000 once losses are fully phased in, but as young people move into work and two-thirds of those in poverty leave it, a share that rises the longer they stay in work, the rise is reversed by around year six. The projection passes the DWP’s own estimate of 50,000 fewer people in poverty around year seven, a figure we use only as a cross-check, and settles at around 135,000 fewer by year 25. Figure 4 shows how this compares across the two measures of poverty that the model reports.

Figure 4: A rise in poverty becomes a fall as young people move into work

Change in the number of people in poverty after housing costs from the whole Milburn Review package, relative to no reform

Notes: Each exit from poverty counts everyone in the household. Growth affects absolute poverty only. The DWP estimate is a cross-check and is not used to set the model.

Source: GGF Calculations using PolicyEngine, Understanding Society, the Milburn Review and DWP.

The two measures diverge because they treat growth differently. Relative poverty counts people living below 60% of the median income in the same year, so when growth raises incomes across the population it lifts the median, and the poverty line with it, by as much as it lifts the incomes of people near the line, which leaves the number in relative poverty unchanged once the employment response is complete. Absolute poverty instead measures incomes against a line held fixed in real terms, so every rise in incomes from growth carries some people over it, and absolute poverty keeps falling, to around 160,000 below the no-reform level by year ten and around 193,000 by year 25. The gap between the two lines is therefore the contribution of growth to poverty reduction, which a relative measure on its own will always miss.

3.1 When is the 50,000 fall in poverty reached?

The DWP’s estimate that the package leaves 50,000 fewer people in relative poverty describes a steady state, with the benefit changes in place and all 440,000 extra young people already in work. Its model has no timeline, so it cannot say when that point is reached. The benefit changes are fully rolled out within around three years, but how quickly poverty falls depends on how quickly young people move into work, and the review itself phases its employment effect in over a decade.

Figure 5 compares two timetables for the same 440,000 jobs. Following the review’s own phasing, on which the DWP estimate rests, poverty is still around 112,000 higher than without the reform when the benefit changes are fully rolled out, and the 50,000 fall is not reached until around year seven. If young people instead move into work at the pace we observe in Understanding Society, poverty falls below its pre-reform level within three years and the 50,000 fall is reached around year four. Both timetables end in the same place, but on the review’s own timetable around 140,000 more people are in poverty at year four, which suggests the speed with which the Youth Guarantee and employment support reach young people matters as much to the package’s poverty record as the benefit changes themselves.

Figure 5: The pace of moves into work decides when poverty falls

Change in relative poverty from the whole Milburn Review package under two timetables for 440,000 extra young people moving into work

Notes: The DWP timetable follows the review’s NEET reduction profile, 2027/28 to 2036/37. The GGF timetable follows observed moves into work in Understanding Society.

Source: GGF Calculations using PolicyEngine, Understanding Society, the Milburn Review and DWP.

The evidence also points to what the model leaves out, since studies that link microsimulation to a model of the whole economy show that reforms which raise labour supply can lift employment while lowering wages12. Using standard estimates of how easily workers of different ages and qualifications substitute for one another13, the review’s 440,000 extra young low-skilled workers could lower similar workers’ wages by around 3%, costing those already in work around £1.6bn a year, about as much as young people gain from growth. Against this, the model does not count the lasting pay penalty that youth unemployment leaves, estimated at 13 to 21 per cent by age 4214, which earlier entry to work partly avoids, nor young people who keep their jobs after turning 25.

These estimates are illustrative rather than a forecast or a full cost-benefit analysis. The largest uncertainty is the package’s replacement support, since the Severe and Complex Needs Insurance, the Additional Cost Allowance and the Health and Disability Fund have no published rates, so both their value and who receives them are best guesses that should be replaced once the payments are costed. The value of the model is that it makes these assumptions visible and shows the gains from reform alongside the losses when a decision is made, which is the evidence the debate on the Milburn Review, and a growth strategy more broadly, needs and does not currently have.

Appendix A. Evidence from Understanding Society

Projecting what happens after young people move into work needs data that follow the same people over many years. We link waves of Understanding Society, the UK’s largest household panel survey, from 2009-10 to 2023-24, around 466,000 person-year records, and identify every move from not working into paid work. For each move we derive hourly pay from earnings and usual hours in 2024 prices, follow the person through later waves to measure how their pay grows relative to the economy average, and link them to their household’s income to see whether the household was in poverty before they started work and whether it left poverty afterwards, after housing costs and counting everyone in the household. Table A1 sets out the estimates the model uses.

Table A1: Estimates from Understanding Society used in the model

Estimate Result
Annual rate of moving into work, NEET 16 to 24-year-olds 31% for those not on disability benefits, 7.5% for those on them
Entry pay, 18 to 24-year-olds £8.91 an hour, around 33 hours a week (2024 prices)
Pay growth above the economy average after entry 4.3% a year aged 18 to 24, 2.4% aged 25 to 34, under 1% from 35
In household poverty before entering work, 18 to 24 33% after housing costs
Out of poverty after entering work, 18 to 24 66% after one year in work, rising to 86% after six

Notes: Poverty is below 60% of median equivalised household income after housing costs, counting everyone in the household.

Source: GGF Calculations using Understanding Society.

Figure A1 shows that young people who enter work see their pay rise much faster than those who enter later, around 50% in real terms over ten years for a 20-year-old against around 10% for someone entering at 42, and each new worker in the model follows the path for their age, net of tax and the Universal Credit taper. Figure A2 shows the share of young people in poverty who are out of it by years in work. Beyond six years, where our data run out, the model lets this share rise slowly towards the 87% observed for all workers aged 25 to 34, closing 39% of the remaining gap each year, the rate at which people in poverty typically leave it.
